Need to search first.I've written notes for most of Exodus 36, but some of what you asked for is missing. My tools were cut off after about a dozen searches, and no attempt to open a full page worked. So everything below comes from the search-result excerpts, which are often cut short. I never reached the NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org or any page on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching, so the notes say nothing about those. The only Catholic source I found is Haydock's commentary, which is hosted on Bible Hub.

Gill's notes appear on more than one site, so here is a key to the short names used below:
- **EW** (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-36/
- **MHC** (Matthew Henry): https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_036.cfm
- **PA** (Precept Austin): https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-36-commentary
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/36.htm
- **Gill:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-36.html
- **Pulpit:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-36.html
- **Pulpit (Spanish):** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/tpc/exodus-36.html. This is a Spanish translation of the Pulpit Commentary, and the only place I got its notes on vv. 22–33.
- **Pulpit Homiletics:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/exodus/36.htm
- **Poole:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/exodus/36.htm
- **JFB** (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/exodus-36.html
- **Haydock** (Catholic): https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/exodus/36.htm

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**Whole chapter (vv. 8–38)**
- Most of the chapter repeats the instructions of chapters 25–30 (vv. 8–38 follow ch. 26 closely). The difference is that things ordered there are now reported as done. Ellicott says the exact repetition teaches that acceptable obedience means keeping God's commands down to the smallest detail. Pulpit says the closeness of the wording shows how exactly they obeyed. (Ellicott; Pulpit)
- Bush (quoted by Precept Austin) says the long list is not tiresome once you see it as a hint that we should keep every detail of God's word. Precept Austin adds that this obedience "to the letter" was enabled by the Spirit and was not legalism. (PA)
- J. Orr says the builders changed nothing in the plans, tried no improvements and added no ornaments. He applies this to work for Christ: we cannot improve on the gospel. (Pulpit Homiletics)
- Guzik quotes Cole: a devout priest would have enjoyed this list the way an architect enjoys going over plans. (EW)

**v. 1**
- This verse introduces the whole section through chapter 39. Ellicott and Pulpit both read it as the work starting under Bezalel and Oholiab's direction, done just as God had commanded. (Ellicott; Pulpit)
- Gill says all the skill came from God. That includes the ordinary workers' ability to learn from the two masters, which God "enlarged" beyond their natural ability. (Gill)
- "Skillful person" is literally "wise of heart." (PA)
- JFB says the workers were driven by obedience, zeal for God's glory and love of his service, not by gain, honour or power. (JFB)

**v. 2**
- Henry and Poole both say that being gifted was not enough; the workers also needed a regular call. Henry says the two things to look for in calling ministers are ability and willingness. (MHC; Poole)
- "Whose heart stirred him" literally means his heart was "lifted up," with his affections set on the work (Clarke, quoted by Guzik; also Precept Austin). (EW; PA)
- Precept Austin notes that God gave the skill, but the workers still had to choose to respond. It also says the verb "come" is the word used for drawing near to God with an offering, and links it to Romans 12:1. (PA)

**v. 3**
- Moses handed over all the gifts, and Gill says he "kept back nothing" for himself. (Gill)
- On "morning after morning," Poole says morning was chosen as the first and best part of the day. Henry turns it into a lesson: our offerings to God, including prayer and praise, should be each morning's work. (Poole; MHC)
- Henry suggests some who held back at first were moved by their neighbours' eagerness, or that some gave a second time. (MHC)
- Ellicott compares this giving with David's collection for the Temple and the gifts in the days of Ezra and Nehemiah. (Ellicott)
- JFB says the building started after the first gifts came in and never had to stop for lack of materials. (JFB)

**vv. 4–5**
- The workers' honesty is the main point. They could have kept the surplus but went together to Moses instead (Gill; Henry; Bush in Precept Austin; JFB). Henry adds that they also refused to take in more than they needed, so they would not be tempted or suspected. (Gill; MHC; PA; JFB)
- Gill says the workers had worked out what the job needed, and wonders which is more remarkable: the people's generosity or the workers' honesty. (Gill)
- Guzik says the planners clearly knew what "enough" was, and that people asked to give should expect the work to be well planned and run. (EW)
- Pulpit and Pett add that the surplus was getting in the workers' way. Pett's commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/exodus-36.html (Pulpit)

**v. 6**
- "Proclamation" is literally "a voice" passing through the camp. Gill says the Targums take this as a herald, and Currid (in Precept Austin) says it shows the message was spoken aloud. (Gill; PA)
- Ellicott reads "make any more work" as meaning the extra gifts were mostly handmade, such as thread and goat-hair yarn. On that reading the poorest givers were the keenest. He asks when Christian giving will ever need to be "restrained." (Ellicott)
- Poole notes that the women did part of this work, as well as the men. (Poole)
- Gill says that instead of needing a push to give, these people had to be held back. (Gill)

**v. 7**
- Gill says the text doesn't say what happened to the surplus. He thinks it was probably stored for later use at the tabernacle. (Gill)
- Guzik says God gives us far more than we need and our giving answers his. He also quotes Cole: those who held back their gifts found God no longer needed them, and so had no share in the work. (EW)

**vv. 8–13 (the linen curtains)**
- These verses follow 26:1–6 closely, with only the verb tenses changed. They describe the inner covering. (Ellicott)
- Gill notes that the text keeps saying "he" did the work. This could mean Moses, who gave the orders, Bezalel as chief director, or each worker in turn. (Gill)
- Henry sees the tent as a picture of the church: on earth but not rooted in it, humble and on the move, beautified by the Spirit's gifts (the embroidery), and made "one tabernacle" out of many parts. (MHC)
- Precept Austin links "so the tabernacle was a unit" (v. 13) with 1 Corinthians 12:20 ("many members, one body"), Ephesians 2:20–22 and 1 Peter 2:4–5. (PA)

**vv. 14–18 (the goat-hair curtains)**
- This is the outer tent covering. The wording is nearly the same as 26:7–11, with two short clauses left out. (Ellicott)
- Poole: these were for the outward covering of the tabernacle. (Poole)

**v. 19 (the outer coverings)**
- This matches 26:14 exactly. (Ellicott)
- Older writers name the top layer differently. Guzik's text says "badger skins," while Ellicott and Pulpit list "seals' skins." (EW; Ellicott; Pulpit, via https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/36-1.htm)
- Henry takes the coverings as a sign of God's protection over his church (Isaiah 4:6). (MHC)
- William Kelly reads them as pictures of Christ (cited at https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/36-3.html):
  - goat hair: Christ "in His prophetic separateness"
  - red rams' skins: his complete dedication to God
  - the outer skins: the power that kept out evil

**vv. 20–34 (frames, bases and crossbars)**
- After the roof come the walls, still in the order of chapter 26. Ellicott says the match with 26:15–29 is closer than the King James Version makes it look. (Ellicott)
- Henry says the boards and bars stand for the church's strength, and the way they lock together stands for believers' unity making it stable. (MHC)
- **v. 22:** Pulpit says the Hebrew is better translated as two tenons set in order against each other, as in 26:17. (Pulpit, Spanish)
- **vv. 27 and 32:** Ellicott and Pulpit say "sides westward" really means the back (west) side. (Ellicott; Pulpit, Spanish)
- **v. 30:** Ellicott says "two under each frame" is clearly the meaning, but the Hebrew here has lost a repeated phrase that appears in 26:25. (Ellicott)
- **v. 33:** Pulpit says the middle bar "reached from end to end," as in 26:28, rather than "shooting through." (Pulpit, Spanish)

**vv. 35–36 (the veil)**
- Poole: this is the inner veil that divided the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. (Poole)
- Henry says the veil showed the "darkness and distance" of the old covenant compared with the New Testament's invitation to come near. It also shows our present state compared with heaven, where we will see God as he is. (MHC)

**vv. 37–38 (the entrance screen)**
- Ellicott says these verses add one new fact to chapter 26: the tops of the five posts were covered with gold. Either God gave no order about this, or Moses didn't record it. (Ellicott)
- Pulpit translates "their capitals and their rods" and notes these had not been mentioned before. Pett also says the capitals and rods are new. (Pulpit)
- Poole says "overlaid with gold" in the earlier passage is a figure of speech: only the tops and the bands were gold, and the rest stayed bare. Haydock agrees that on some parts of the posts the wood showed. (Poole; Haydock)
- Henry says people gathered at this door even though they could not go in. While we live here, we must get as near to God as we can. (MHC)

---

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

I found no sources from different traditions clearly disagreeing about this chapter. These are the closest I came:
- **Calling ministers (v. 2):** Gill, a Baptist, says workers in the church need a call "both from the Lord and from the church." Henry, a Presbyterian nonconformist, speaks of "extraordinary" calls (prophets, apostles) and "ordinary" calls (pastors, teachers). This is more a difference in emphasis than a disagreement. (Gill; MHC)
- **Church funding (v. 1):** the Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary says the command was that Israel as a church should support itself, not that the state should pay for the church. This bears on the old argument between state churches and voluntary giving, though the page doesn't name the commentator's denomination. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/36-1.html
- **Methodist:** Wesley's notes on this chapter came up only as an outline listing the curtains, boards, bars, veil and door hanging. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-moses-called-exodus/
- I found nothing from Lutheran, Pentecostal or Anglican teachers on this chapter.

---

## 3. Other views

**Catholic (Haydock)**
- **v. 3:** Haydock calls the gifts "first-fruits," the best of everything. He reads the people's eagerness as partly making amends for their generosity toward the golden calf. Pett and the Expositor's Bible say something similar from the Protestant side: the giving showed repentance, or hearts "purified" by punishment and shame.
  - Pett: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/exodus-36.html
  - Expositor's Bible: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/exodus-36.html
- **Teaching through pastors:** Worthington, quoted by Haydock, says materials are useless unless handled well, and in the same way Scripture doesn't teach us unless God teaches us through his pastors (Ephesians 4).
- **Bars (vv. 31–33):** Haydock notes that Josephus mentions a bar across the west end.
- **Repetition:** Calmet, also quoted by Haydock, thinks Moses may have given each worker plans, which would explain why so much is repeated.
- Source for all of the above: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/exodus/36.htm

**Modern scholarship, Orthodox teaching and popular movements:** I couldn't reach any sources for these, so I've left them out.
